title: The picture behind every picture
summary: The graph of w = f(z) needs four numbers; every picture on the site is one of its shadows: two planes tied by a clock, a painted plane, the real and imaginary surfaces, the root staircase and the sphere.

music.prompt: Calm, spacious instrumental for a maths explainer: soft piano and warm synth pads, slow and curious, no drums, gentle rise when the pictures turn.

segments.text: The graph of w equals f of z needs four numbers: x and y for where z sits, u and v for where w lands. Nobody can draw four dimensions. So every picture in this course is a shadow of that one object, seen from a different side. Here are five.

First shadow: two flat planes, tied by a clock. Draw a stroke on the z plane, and its image appears on the w plane, point for point. Dark is early, bright is late, so matching dots match in time. Zoom in on one dot: where f has a derivative, a tiny square stays a tiny square, turned and stretched.

Second shadow: keep only the z plane, and paint the missing numbers onto it. Where you stand is the Cartesian address of z. The colour there is the polar address of w: hue is its angle, brightness is its length. Red means along the positive real axis, black means zero. For z squared, the colours go round twice.

Third shadow: height u gives the real surface. Turn it a quarter turn inside four dimensions, and the height becomes v: the imaginary surface. The colour is the number we left out, and it trades places with the height. Same object, seen from a new side.

Fourth shadow: a root. The cube root has three values at every point, and this surface holds all three. Walk once round the origin and you land on the next sheet; three laps bring you home. A branch is one sheet, cut along the positive real axis, so the root is smooth across the negative one.

Fifth shadow: wrap the plane onto a sphere, so infinity becomes one point, the north pole. The circle through zero, centre one, radius one, lands on a circle through the south pole. Now one over z is a half-turn about the axis through one and minus one. Zero and infinity swap, and the circle opens into a line.

That is five pictures, one object: two planes tied by a clock, a painted plane, the real and imaginary surfaces, the staircase, the sphere. When a question asks for the image of a shape, you are reading one shadow. Turn the object, and you can see the others.
